name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got a hundred and eighty sows, farrow to finish, which means we breed the piglets and keep them right through until they go for meat. And four hundred acres of wheat and barley, most of which goes back into the pigs as feed. My day starts at six in the farrowing house, checking which sows have pigged overnight, then I do the planning and the figures while Piotr and Kerry do the feeding and washing down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good batch, when twelve piglets come off a sow and every one of them makes it. I keep a little chart on the office wall and I'm ridiculously pleased when the line goes up. What wears me out is the smell in my hair and the price, which the processor sets every Friday and which I can't argue with.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you, at work and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Joe, my husband, drove lorries for thirty years and now he runs the combine and the grain dryer and complains about both. Two staff, Piotr who's been with us nine years, and Kerry who's twenty-four and better with pigs than I was at her age. Our twins are thirty and both live in town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My niece set it up on my laptop last winter. I use it to draft letters to the bank and once to check a feed ration when the nutritionist was on holiday. I double-checked the ration with him after, mind you, and it was close but not right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for the boring bits and leave it at that. I'd tell the women at the pig group it's good for writing to the bank, not for anything with a heartbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing. If prices and hiring carry on the same, the thing that hurts me is still the processor setting my price on a Friday afternoon. AI doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it a bit more for the paperwork, maybe an hour saved a week. Replace the old feed bin on the finishing shed, which I've budgeted at six thousand. Get Kerry onto the pig vet course in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slightly bored, if anything. It's another gadget, and I've seen a lot of gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour a week you saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Probably sit in the farrowing house with a coffee and watch the litters. Joe says that's not work. I say a sow that sees you every day is a calmer sow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the pig group who'd see it differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would. He's got two thousand sows and he'll buy anything with a screen on it. He'll be telling us all it's the future, and then ringing me to ask how to work it.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's useful for the boring bits and leave it at that. I'd say at the pig group it's good for letters to the bank, not anything with a heartbeat.
S0.think: Nothing really changes for me. The thing that hurts is still the processor setting my price every Friday, and AI doesn't fix that.
S0.do: Uses AI a little more for paperwork, saving about an hour a week. Replaces the finishing shed feed bin for about six thousand and sends her young stockperson Kerry on the pig vet course in spring.
S0.feel: Fine and slightly bored, as if it's one more gadget among many.
S0.quote: I say a sow that sees you every day is a calmer sow.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is organised and dry, and judges tools by results, not hype. Her anger is saved for the processor's pricing, not technology. She would spend any saved time with the animals, which tells you what she values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: fewer jobs for beginners is a choice companies make, not the weather. If the big processors save money, there should be rules that some of it goes into apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a slow change, and slow suits me. I'll see what works on Gareth's farm first. What bothers me is Kerry. Fewer beginner jobs means people like her never get a start, and she nearly didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sign up for the camera system that spots lame pigs, once two or three farms in the group have tried it. Probably three thousand a year. Keep both staff. Maybe take on a school leaver for a summer, because if nobody else is hiring young people, somebody has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I can see it coming, and that helps. Slow I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kerry nearly didn't get a start. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She left college and applied to the big pig company over the hill, and they said she needed two years' experience. Two years! I took her on because Piotr knew her mum. If I hadn't, she'd be stacking shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a camera that spots lame pigs do part of Kerry's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part. She walks the pens and checks legs twice a day. If the camera does the first look, she can spend more time on the ones that need it. That's how I'd sell it to her, anyway, and I think it's true.

S1.say: Fewer jobs for beginners is a choice companies make, not the weather. If the big processors save money, rules should make some of it go into apprenticeships.
S1.think: Slow change suits me, and I'll watch what works on Gareth's farm first. What bothers me is young people like Kerry, who nearly didn't get a start.
S1.do: Signs up for a camera system that spots lame pigs, at about three thousand a year, once a few farms in her group have tried it. Keeps both staff and takes on a school leaver for a summer.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but steadied by being able to see it coming and plan.
S1.quote: She left college and applied to the big pig company over the hill, and they said she needed two years' experience. Two years!
S1.fieldNote: Her politics come through as practical demands, like apprenticeships funded from savings. She will adopt technology, but only after others prove it. She frames the camera as helping Kerry rather than replacing her, and seems to believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office workers need a union and a government with a spine. And the politicians arguing loudly should stop arguing and do something, like taxing the companies that cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd use one of those assistants for the farm office myself. The pig records, the medicine book, the grain contracts. It'd save Joe and me a whole evening a week. So I'd be cheering for the workers and buying the thing that replaces them. I'm aware of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the farm office assistant, probably at a few hundred a year, once the pig group says it's safe with our data. Move my bank account to a branch that still has people in it. And phone the twins, because Lucy works in an accounts department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Lucy. For us, it'd be a relief to get the evenings back, and I feel a bit guilty about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be cheering for workers and buying the replacement. How do you live with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, I suppose. But I'm not the one firing anyone, I'm doing my own paperwork faster. The difference is who loses a wage. On my farm, nobody does. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucy if she rang you upset?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she should come home for Sunday dinner and we'd work it out on the back of an envelope. She's got savings, she's thirty. I'd tell her to look at the jobs the new rules create before she panics. And to join the union now, not after.

S2.say: Office workers need a union and a government with a spine. The politicians should stop arguing and tax the companies that cut staff.
S2.think: I'd buy one of those assistants for the farm office myself and get an evening a week back. So I'd be cheering for workers and buying the thing that replaces them, and I know it.
S2.do: Buys a farm office assistant for a few hundred a year once her pig group says it's safe with farm data. Moves to a bank branch that still has staff and calls her daughter Lucy, who works in accounts.
S2.feel: Anxious for her daughter, and quietly relieved and a bit guilty about getting evenings back.
S2.quote: So I'd be cheering for the workers and buying the thing that replaces them. I'm aware of that.
S2.fieldNote: She names her own contradiction before I can, which is typical of her. She settles it by drawing a line at whether anyone loses a wage on her farm. Her worry here lands on her daughter Lucy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a fair tax system. If shares and houses boom and ordinary people lose their jobs, the gains have to be shared, through tax, through public services, whatever it takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, our land would go up and so would the bit of shares Joe's got from his pension. We'd be better off on paper. But pork prices would fall if people lost their jobs and stopped buying the good stuff. So I'm not sure we'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lock in a feed price for the year, because grain markets would go mad. Fix the contract with the processor for twelve months if they'd let me. Put a bit of money aside for the twins in case either needs a deposit or a rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Not scared for us, but it'd feel like watching people you know get hurt while your house goes up in value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the pig group would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, funnily enough. He's borrowed millions for his new sheds. If the bank gets jumpy, he's in trouble. I don't like the man much, but I'd hate to see him go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want the gains shared. Would you pay more tax yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it went somewhere I could see. A hospital, the bus back to our village, school dinners. Not if it vanished into a big pot. I've paid tax for forty years and I'd like to see the receipt.

S3.say: This is exactly why we need a fair tax system. If shares and houses boom while ordinary people lose jobs, the gains have to be shared through tax and public services.
S3.think: We'd be better off on paper, with land and Joe's pension shares going up. But pork prices would fall if people stopped buying the good stuff, so I'm not sure we'd come out ahead.
S3.do: Locks in a feed price for the year and tries to fix a twelve-month contract with the processor. Sets money aside for the twins in case either needs help with a deposit or rent.
S3.feel: Unsettled, like watching people you know get hurt while your house goes up in value.
S3.quote: I've paid tax for forty years and I'd like to see the receipt.
S3.fieldNote: Her support for taxing the gains comes with a condition: she wants to see where the money goes. She thinks about the knock-on effect on pork demand, which shows how closely she follows her market. Her sympathy for a rival she dislikes was unexpected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in pig sheds have to come with rules. Animal welfare checks, and a guarantee that the people who lose their jobs get paid properly to retrain. Otherwise it's just the big firms taking everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the robots would come for Piotr's job before mine, and Kerry's. Washing down, feeding, moving pigs. That's what scares me. I'd be the boss of a shed full of machines and two people I can't afford to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait six months and watch what happens on Gareth's farm, like always. Then maybe buy a washing robot, because nobody likes washing pens. Promise Piotr and Kerry their jobs for at least two years, in writing, and sit down with Joe about selling up at sixty-two instead of sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I've watched sows for forty years, and a machine can learn the feeding, but I don't think it can learn which sow is about to turn on her piglets. I'd worry for the animals as well as the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Piotr's got a mortgage and two kids at school, and a promise on the yard isn't worth much to a bank. If I write it, he can show it. And it would hold me to it when Joe starts doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow suits you. What happens if you can't wait and watch this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be making decisions blind, and I hate that. I'd probably still go slower than everyone else and lose money doing it. I'd rather lose money than lose Piotr.

S4.say: Robots in pig sheds have to come with rules, like welfare checks and proper pay for people to retrain. Otherwise it's just the big firms taking everything.
S4.think: The robots would come for Piotr's and Kerry's jobs before mine. I'd be the boss of a shed full of machines and two people I can't afford to keep.
S4.do: Waits six months to see results on Gareth's farm, then perhaps buys a pen-washing robot. Promises both staff their jobs for at least two years in writing and discusses selling up at sixty-two with Joe.
S4.feel: A bit sick, worried for the animals as well as the people, and unhappy about deciding without proof.
S4.quote: I'd rather lose money than lose Piotr.
S4.fieldNote: Her usual wait-and-see approach gets squeezed when the change is fast, and she knows it. The written promise is a smart, practical move that also binds her against her husband's arithmetic. Her concern for the sows' welfare runs right alongside her concern for her staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help is a law that says if you put a robot in, you pay into a fund for the person it replaced, for retraining or a pension top-up. And independent welfare checks on robot sheds, so animals don't get treated like boxes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who sets the price. All these pictures, the price for my pigs is still set by three processors on a Friday. If robots make pork cheaper, I bet that doesn't reach the farmer or the shopper. Somebody in the middle keeps it.

headlineQuote: I'd rather lose money than lose Piotr.
portrait: Fatima Lopez is fifty-eight and runs a hundred and eighty sows and four hundred acres of grain with her husband Joe and two staff, Piotr and Kerry. She is organised, dry and left-leaning, and she uses AI tools now and then for letters and checks, but always waits to see a neighbour try something first. Through the office scenarios she admits she would buy the tools that replace office workers while cheering for those workers. The robot picture hits her through her staff, and she would put their jobs in writing for two years. Underneath every scenario sits her real grudge: the processors who set her price every Friday.
biggestWorry: The fast robots picture, because the jobs of her two staff, Piotr and Kerry, would go first, and she wouldn't have time to wait and see.
whatWouldHelp: A law making firms that install robots pay into a fund for the replaced worker's retraining or pension, plus independent welfare checks on robot-run sheds.
